title: Below the Line
passages:
The Marrow groaned as the wave caught her beam-on, rail burying until green water washed the deck. Sol didn't wait for the roll-back. She was already moving, one hand on the shrouds, the other snatching the coiled heaving-line from the pinrail where it lived for exactly this. Nia beat her to the boat-hook, aluminum shaft warm from the sun they'd had at noon, and didn't ask what to do — just ran the hook out over the stanchion, braced her boots on the wet nonskid, and waited for the next wallow to bring the water up to them.

"There — starboard quarter, twenty meters!" Wren's voice cracked over the deck speaker, thin with cold and the wind stealing words. She stood frozen at the winch, slate dark in her hand, the drum silent behind her.

Sol didn't look up. "Got him. Nia, hook the collar. I'll take the line."

The boat-hook dipped, caught, missed, caught again on the second roll — the orange webbing of Dey's harness, torn loose from its tether. Nia's arms locked, shoulders hiked to her ears, hauling dead weight through water that didn't want to give him up. Sol took the line two-handed, walking it back hand-over-hand, boots sliding on the deck's cant. The Marrow heaved the other way, rail lifting, and the water rushed off like a flushed tank, leaving Dey dangling in the hook's grip, half-in half-out, a seal pup caught in a net.

"Steady!" Sol barked, and Nia planted herself, muscles jumping under her soaked jacket.

They swung him inboard together on the next roll, a graceless tangle of limbs and rope, and dropped him on the nonskid like a sack of wet cement. Dey didn't gasp. Didn't cough. His lips were the gray of old ash, eyes open but fixed on nothing, pupils blown wide against the dim. Water bubbled at the corner of his mouth, thin and slow. His chest moved — barely — a reflex the deep hadn't finished killing yet.

"Dey." Sol dropped beside him, fingers finding carotid, wrist, the soft place under the jaw. Pulse thready, skin cold as the bilge. "Dey, look at me."

His eyes didn't shift. Didn't blink. The storm screamed in the rigging and the Marrow took another hit, but the man on the deck didn't flinch, didn't shrink, didn't do anything a living body should do when the world tries to shake it apart.

Nia crouched on his other side, face pale in the running lights, one hand hovering over his chest like she wanted to press down and couldn't decide where. "He's heavy," she said, quiet. "Too heavy. Like the water's still in him."

Sol's jaw tightened. She peeled back Dey's eyelid with a thumb, watched the pupil stay round and dead. "The deep doesn't let go easy. Wren — get the slate. Now."

Wren didn't move. The winch drum sat silent behind her, the slack line coiling in the scuppers like a dead snake. Her slate glowed faint in her hand, the same eleven seconds she'd found in her own record blinking steady at the top of the build.

"Wren!" Sol's voice cracked the wind. "The slate. His slate. Read it."

Wren came off the winch like something had cut her loose.

She dropped to her knees on the wet nonskid, took Dey's collar in both hands, and thumbed the housing clip on the slate puck — a gray disc the size of a saucer, strapped where a diver's throat meets the harness, writing down depth and air and pulse whether the diver likes it or not. Her fingers found the gasket, found water beaded in the seam, and she swore once, softly, at the water.

"Talk while you work," Sol said.

"This is my talking face."

She seated the puck in the cradle on her own slate, the little dock that pulls a diver's record out and lays it flat, and the screen filled with a green ladder of numbers. Behind her the drum sat dead, its slack line slithering in the scuppers with every roll.

"Fourteen fifty-two, he's on the rail," Wren said. "No loop, no scrubber, no canister on his chest to take the carbon dioxide back out of his breath. One lungful and a bad idea. He's at forty-one meters by fifteen-oh-four, which is faster than I go with a rig and air." She stopped. "He was trying to get somewhere before something happened."

"What happened," Nia said.

"That's the problem." Wren dragged the timeline open with her thumb. "The slate kept writing the whole way down. Depth, air, heart rate, fifty-one minutes of it. There's just nothing underneath the numbers. No sound, no picture, no voice. Not corrupted. Not jammed. *Empty.*"

Sol's hand was still on Dey's jaw, holding his head out of the roll. "Meaning what."

"Meaning below thirty meters he stopped laying anything down." Wren looked up, rain running into her collar. "You know the line. Thirty meters, give or take. Under it the deep doesn't hurt you, it just stops filing. Whatever you did down there never gets written, so there's nothing for me to rebuild. I don't lose an hour and hand it back. I can't find it to begin with. Nobody comes up from under the line with the hour still on them."

"So he gets out of his debt for free," Nia said. She had Dey's wrist between two fingers, counting, her face doing nothing at all. "Forty-one meters. That's the pocket, isn't it. That's Rusk's pharmacy."

"He got there," Wren said. "And it took the rest."

"Then don't tell me what's missing." Sol sat back on her heels. "Tell me it's a cut."

That was the thing Wren did. A cut left a seam — so she ran the seam check without being asked, laying Dey's record against every other clock on the boat that had watched the same hour: the inclinometer in the masthead, the deck camera's counter, the drum's encoder up on the winch housing. Two clocks that disagree by half a second mean a hand was in there with a blade. Two clocks that agree and leave the middle blank mean nobody touched it.

The check came back in four seconds. Every clock on the Marrow agreed. The middle was blank.

"Water," she said. "It's water. Nothing was edited."

She heard herself say it and felt the floor of her stomach go, because she had run this same check last night on a different slate and gotten the other answer.

Dey's mouth moved. His eyes stayed fixed on the rain, but his jaw worked, and what came out was not a word a half-drowned man should have breath for.

"Wren."

Nia's counting fingers stopped. "That's twice now."

On the console above them the backup channel — the emergency band, the one that carries four hundred meters and no further — opened with a hiss, and the man at forty-two meters said her name again, patient as a man reading off a list.

Wren killed the deck speaker with the back of her hand, but the name hung there anyway, the way a struck bell hangs.

"He knows me," she said.

"Everybody knows the tech," Nia said, not looking up from Dey's wrist. "You're the one who talks to the dead men's slates."

"I've never given a diver my name. I've never met a man at forty-two meters." Wren's thumb was already moving, pulling last night's traffic up out of the console. "And I've got a worse problem, which is that I know his."

She let it play.

The recording came thin under the storm-static, but the voice on it was hers — flat and winded, the way she sounded when she was working. *At pocket. Seal intact. I see it.* A pause, her own breathing loud in the mic. Then smaller, turned away from the boat, toward someone: *I'll bring the winch. I swear it.*

Nobody said anything. The water ran off the deck, and Dey's chest went up and came down.

"That's last night," Sol said finally. "You slept in the chair last night. I watched you."

"I don't remember recording it." Wren set the slate on the nonskid, carefully, like it might go off. "There's a fifty-two-minute hole in my own deck log. Sealed shut by my own hand, in my own method. I went down there. I came back up. And then I cut the whole thing out of myself, and I don't remember doing that either."

Sol's face didn't move, but her grip on Dey's jaw did.

"Then that settles it," she said. "Nobody goes near that tower. We ride it out, we—"

"Ride it out on what." Nia said it flat, the way you'd read a gauge. "Rusk is back at first light for the case or the boat. Teo has one cartridge left after what Rusk pocketed. There's no tomorrow to ride into."

Sol's mouth shut.

"The pocket's the only score in four hundred meters," Wren said. "Sealed pharmacy, forty-two meters, dry as a bone. It's why Dey went. It's why Rusk dangled it. One pull of that and we buy the berths and pay the debt and keep the Marrow." She was already doing the sum and hating the answer. "But somebody has to bring it up. And here's the part nobody wants."

She crossed to the rig locker, spun the dogs, and hauled it open on three dive suits hanging orange and scarred, their umbilicals coiled at the collars — the hoses that carry air down and a voice back up. She put her hand flat on the first chest seal.

"Thirty-meter rating. This one too. This one." She slapped each in turn. "Past thirty the seal creeps. You take water into the suit at forty-two and it's not a rescue, it's a dredge." She looked at Sol. "There's one suit on this boat rated to forty-two. It's mine. So it's me or it's nobody, and nobody leaves a girl's brother to die for arithmetic."

"There's a cost," Sol said quietly. "You know the line. You go under thirty, you come up missing the swim. Like Dey. Like me."

"I know." Wren pulled her own suit off its hook, the deep-rated one, heavier than the rest. "I did it last night and I'm still missing it. So I'll do it again, and lose this one too, and somebody topside is going to have to explain to me why we're all crying when I break the surface."

She sat on the deck coaming and shoved her legs in. Behind her the drum sat dead with one good pull left in it, and every soul on deck knew it, and nobody said it.

"I'm going down," she said. "Keep the channel open. If he says my name again, write down what else he says."

Sol didn't argue. She never did when the numbers only had one answer. She crossed the heaving deck to the winch housing, kicked the slack line clear of the scuppers, and planted her boots on the diamond plate where Wren had stood a minute before. The drum was a rust-streaked cylinder, its hydraulic motor whining low under the storm's groan, the pressure gauge on its flank pegged in the yellow since the cold-case pull.

"One pull," she said to the drum, like she was telling a dog to stay. "That's what you've got. Make it count."

She flipped the manual override, the big red lever that bypassed the hydraulics and put the drum on muscle and ratchet. The handle folded out with a clang, steel thick as her wrist. Sol took it two-handed, braced her shoulders against the frame, and tested the bite. The drum held. The line — spliced where the old umbilical had parted on the Mercy General job, a knot Wren had tied and whip-finished with her own hands — came taut with a sound like a cello string.

"Air," Sol called over her shoulder, not looking up. "Last bottle. Green band. Top shelf, port locker."

Nia was already moving, unclipping the high-pressure hose from the manifold where it fed the deck repressurization panel. She hauled the bottle down — a gray cylinder the size of a fire extinguisher, its gauge needle sitting sweet in the green — and ran the hose back to the winch, threading it through the fairlead Sol had welded into the drum's cheek plate for exactly this. A spliced line couldn't carry a voice past forty meters. But it could carry air, if you fed it slow and didn't mind the taste of oil and old rubber.

"Regulator's on the end," Nia said, clamping the hose to the line with zip-ties she'd cut with her teeth. "Push-to-talk on the comms box. You've got maybe ninety minutes at forty-two if you breathe like you're sleeping. Less if you work."

Wren stood in her deep-rated suit, orange collar open, helmet cradled in the crook of her arm. The suit was heavier than the others, its chest plate reinforced with a second layer of kevlar weave, its umbilical port fitted with a double O-ring seal that had passed a forty-five-meter chamber test three months ago. She'd watched the test. She'd signed the log. She didn't remember either.

"Ninety minutes," she said. "And the pull."

"One pull," Sol repeated. "I crank, you come up. You stop, I crank harder. The drum doesn't know mercy and neither do I."

She spun the ratchet handle once, testing. The line sang, a high thin note that the wind stole. The spliced knot — a double fisherman's, tight as a fist — passed through the fairlead clean.

"Channel's open," Nia said, tapping the comms box mounted on the winch frame. "Backup band. Salas is still transmitting. Dey's slate is dead weight but the puck's still warm if you want it."

Wren shook her head. "Extra drag. I know the tower."

"Do you." Sol's voice was flat. "Because last night you knew it well enough to tie that knot and swear you'd bring the winch. And this morning you don't remember the swim."

"I know the way to the pocket." Wren snapped her collar shut, the seal hissing home. "I know the rule. Thirty meters and the deep stops filing. I'll lose the dive. That's the deal."

"Then here's the rest of it." Sol leaned on the ratchet handle, taking the drum's weight on her arms. "You come up without the medicine, I cut the line. You come up with Salas and no medicine, I cut the line. You come up with the medicine and no Salas —" She stopped. The Marrow took a hit that drove the rail under, green water exploding across the deck, and Sol didn't budge, boots welded to the plate. "You come up with the medicine. That's the only version where the line stays."

Wren's helmet sealed with a sound like a coffin lid. Her voice came through the comms box thin and metallic. "Understood. One pull. Ninety minutes. Don't stop cranking."

"Never stopped a day in my life." Sol's hands settled on the handle, knuckles white. "Go on then. The water's waiting."

Wren stepped to the rail, hooked the spliced line's bitter end to her chest D-ring, and went over the side without looking back. The line paid out smooth, the air hose kissing the water behind it, and the drum sang its high thin song as Sol Ferreira began to turn.

The water took the storm off her one meter at a time.

At five she still had the wind in the helmet, and the ratchet going somewhere overhead like a man cracking walnuts, one tooth at a time. At ten the Marrow's bottom slid past her lamp — weed along the keel, the sacrificial zinc, the little block of metal bolted to the hull that rots instead of the hull, worn down to a gray nub. At fourteen the daylight quit.

"Fourteen," Sol said in her ear. The push-to-talk was a rubber nub under her thumb; that was the only way a voice had ever come down an umbilical. "Rate's good. Boots out, let the drum do the work."

Mercy General came up out of the murk at eighteen, nine floors of drowned hospital with the glass long gone out of the curtain wall, the stairwells packed with silt like a chimney full of ash. Wren put her lamp on the east face and counted window bays out loud, because a count said out loud exists somewhere.

"Talk," Sol said.

"I'm counting."

"I don't care what you're doing. Noise means air's passing. Quiet means I start cranking."

"You're a real comfort at eighteen meters."

At twenty-six the cold got in at her wrists and the back of her neck, where the seals always tell you first. She was halfway through a sentence about the east face and could not find the end of it, or the reason she'd started it.

"Thirty," Sol said. "You're on the line now."

The slate on Wren's wrist had gone flat. Her pulse at thirty point one, and under that nothing at all, the way a clerk walks out in the middle of a column and never comes back.

"Nia. You writing?"

"Grease pencil, chart table." Nia's voice was close to the mic, wind tearing at it. "Say your name and what you're doing."

"Wren Achebe. Thirty-one meters, going down the spliced line to the pharmacy pocket at forty-two for Teo's medicine." She heard herself and thought she sounded reasonable, which was the worst part. "Also there's a man down there who knows my name and I never gave it to him. Write down that I said all that in a normal voice."

"Written. Underlined twice."

The backup band — the emergency channel, four hundred meters and no further — opened with a hiss, and this time it didn't just carry him, it carried her.

"Wren."

She thumbed the nub. "Ivo Salas. How do you know my name."

"You gave it to me."

"Try again."

"Last night." His voice was slow and wet at the edges, a man talking around a mouthpiece that wasn't built for talking. "You came down to the seal with a lamp and you put your hand flat on the glass, and you told me your name, and you made me say it back three times. Then you said if you came again not knowing it, I was to say it first, and you'd believe me."

"That's not a plan." Wren's chest plate ticked as the pressure came up on it. "That's leaving a note with a stranger."

"Everything else on this tower rots." A breath, dragged. "Names keep. I've had a year to find out what keeps."

Sol's voice came over the top of his: "Forty point five. Say something."

"I'm here." Wren watched her exhaust go up past the lamp in silver beads. "I'm here, I'm breathing, and the dead man says I set him up to hold my name for me."

"Then he's the most useful man on this coast," Sol said. "Keep him talking."

"Ivo. Say it again. All of it."

He did, patient as a man reading off a list, and while he talked Wren checked her wrist because a tech checks: twenty-two minutes on the slate. Twenty-two. She could account for nine.

"Sol." Her own voice sounded far off in the helmet. "How long since I went over?"

"Twenty-two minutes. Why."

Because nine of them were gone, and she hadn't felt the door shut.

"Nine minutes," Wren said. "Nia, write nine."

"Written."

"Write that it didn't hurt. Write that I didn't feel a door shut, or a cold spot, or anything a person could point at later." She put her lamp down the line. "Write that I'd do it again for less."

"Keep him talking," Sol said. "Both of you."

"Ivo. Say my name and then say what I told you."

"Wren Achebe." The band hissed. His breathing came behind the words, wet, unhurried, a man with nowhere to be. "You said the girl with the pencil was to write down everything, because you'd be the one who couldn't."

"Written," Nia said, from a long way off.

Wren went down. Boot, boot, hand over hand, her left glove fending off the curtain wall where the mullions stood up out of the silt like the ribs of something. Sol called the numbers and she answered each one so the air kept moving.

Thirty-eight. Forty. Forty-one.

Mercy General's pharmacy wasn't a room. It was a pod, a stainless box built into the core of the building and dogged shut with a gasket door, made to hold its own pressure when the water came for everything else. That was the whole reason Rusk had dangled it. A pod like that stayed dry for a hundred years if nobody opened it.

Her wrist slate read forty-two point oh, and under her pulse, nothing. The clerk had walked out again.

She was counting window bays and had lost the count somewhere she couldn't find the start of.

"Forty-two," Sol said. "You're on the bottom. Talk."

Her lamp found the pod at the end of a short corridor, hinges furred green, the laminated glass port the size of a dinner plate still a window instead of a hole. Behind the glass, black. The dogging handle had a lanyard of orange whipping twine around it, three turns and a tuck, whip-finished tight.

Every tech on the coast finishes a line that way. Wren had taught two of them herself. She could have picked her own knot out of a hundred in a dark room, which was the problem, because this was hers.

Her hand went to it. She didn't send it. She was still deciding whether to touch the thing when her fingers found the tail, took up the slack, and pulled, and the knot came apart for them the way a lock comes apart for a key that lives in the house.

Wren looked at the twine in her glove.

"I didn't tell my hands to do that," she said.

"Say again." Sol's voice, flat, with the ratchet going under it, one tooth at a time.

"I untied my own knot without deciding to untie it." She turned the twine over. Nine inches of it, orange, salt-stiff. "Last night I tied this so I'd know the pod. That's all it's for. A mark that says I was here." She stopped. "It's not a mark for me. I'm the one who can't remember. So who's it for."

"Twenty-four minutes," Nia said. "Air's good. Wren, your hands are shaking on the slate, I can see the numbers move."

"Because they're cold, and because I'm about to open a hundred-year-old seal with a body that's had nine minutes taken out of it." Wren put the twine in her thigh pocket, sealed the flap, and set both gloves on the dogging handle. "Ivo, when I open this, keep talking. If I stop answering, you tell Sol what I said and she cranks."

"I always talk," Salas said. "It's the only thing I've got left to spend."

She broke the seal. The pod breathed out at her, a hundred years of dry cold in one gray sigh, and her lamp went through the port into shelves, into a wall of white cases stenciled in a hand she could read from here, and she started to say the word *medicine* —

Then a second lamp came on at the far end of the corridor, low down, near the deck, and started toward her through the silt. The man behind it said her name the way a man reads off a list he has kept for a year.
